scope: Office sequence v3 (14 s): c03_04 + c03_05 as three connected beats — business spending, insufficient revenue, dependence on investor funding (agreement, then receipt)
ledger: kit/finstate.Ledger(start=13).spend(ADVERTISING 2, PAYROLL 1, SERVERS 1).earn(REVENUE 1); funding +20 at month 2 — every on-screen figure derives from it

beat.narration: They were spending heavily on advertising, employees and infrastructure

meaning.what: BigCart pays out its cash on three kinds of cost at once.
meaning.why: Dot-com firms spent ahead of revenue to grab market share.
meaning.consequence: The pile on the founder's desk shrinks visibly: $13M to $9M in one month.

shots.understanding: Spending is real money leaving the company, and it buys recognisable things: a TV commercial, salaries, servers.
shots.focal_point: the cash pile and counter (left), with each destination lighting up as it is named
shots.camera: one composition with a slow 3.5% push; the eye is led by the bills, not by cuts

graphics.why: money must read as money; one figure source

graphics.what: TV commercial (courier delivers a BigCart parcel, end card with offer)
graphics.why: advertising shown as an actual advert

graphics.what: PAY envelopes land on desks; a server rack is wheeled in and powers up
graphics.why: salaries and infrastructure as recognisable actions

shots.rationale: The three costs are one idea (spending), so they share one connected composition with progressive actions instead of three cuts.

beat.narration: without earning enough revenue to sustain themselves

meaning.what: Monthly money out ($4M) is four times money in ($1M).
meaning.why: Revenue had not caught up with the spending.
meaning.consequence: At a $3M monthly shortfall, BigCart's cash runs out in about three months.

shots.understanding: The imbalance, its size, and when it becomes fatal.
shots.focal_point: the SHORTFALL bracket, then the cash line hitting zero
shots.camera: near-static (2% drift) so the viewer can read
shots.lighting: dimmed office plate behind clean panels

graphics.what: money out (by category) vs money in, SHORTFALL -$3M every month
graphics.why: a chart explains the mechanism more clearly than any metaphor

graphics.what: BigCart's cash line Jan→Mar, projected to zero ('cash runs out')

shots.rationale: Educational clarity beats metaphor here; figures are labelled illustrative and come from the ledger.

meaning.what: An investor agrees to fund BigCart: the term sheet is signed and hands are shaken.
meaning.why: Without new money the company would soon run out of cash.
meaning.consequence: A promise of capital, not yet money in the bank.

shots.understanding: The company's fate is decided by investors; the agreement is a separate step from receiving money.
shots.focal_point: the pen on the term sheet, then the handshake

graphics.what: TERM SHEET — Investment $20M, signature drawn on 'investors'

graphics.why: separates the agreement from the receipt of money for muted viewing

shots.rationale: Interaction (making the case, signing, shaking hands) instead of characters rotating joints in place.

meaning.what: The $20M wire arrives; the cash pile and counter jump from $4M to $24M.
meaning.why: Investors delivered the money they agreed to provide.
meaning.consequence: The cash line jumps, then falls again toward 'next round needed' — survival depends on continuing funding.

shots.understanding: Capital entering the business, and why it must keep coming.
shots.focal_point: the wire slip, then the jump on the cash line

graphics.why: receipt of capital, distinct from the agreement

graphics.what: same cash chart as beat B: +$20M jump, then line toward 'next round needed'
graphics.why: continuity of one indicator across beats
names the second step of funding for muted viewing

shots.rationale: Returns to beat B's chart (same geometry) so the viewer sees the consequence of funding on the indicator they already understand.
